syllabus.clause: the frame table, pin counts and dirty bits; eviction policies (LRU-K, CLOCK, 2Q); latches (short, physical) vs locks (transactional). Modern designs avoid the hash-table indirection: LeanStore pointer swizzling (ICDE 2018) and vmcache (SIGMOD 2023). Contrast with the mmap approach (Ch.12).

items.item: The fully pinned pool claim uses a pool sized to exactly the number of pages already loaded, so the rejection is a genuine capacity failure with zero evictable frames, not an edge case sensitive to how many unpinned frames happen to remain.

at.step: Build a real buffer pool: a frame table, a pin count per frame, a dirty bit per frame. Pin every single frame in the pool, then try to load one more page than the pool can hold. What happens?

items.item: The dirty-write-back measurement checks the write-back log's own last entry against the specific page id that was evicted, not merely that the log's length increased, so the claim is specifically that the correct page was flushed, not just that some flush happened.

items.item: The CLOCK demonstration deliberately re-accesses one specific frame between two separate eviction-triggering loads, rather than relying on initial load order alone, since a naive sweep would otherwise evict whichever frame the clock hand happens to reach first, which would not demonstrate the reference bit's own protective effect at all.

at.step: Measured: CLOCK genuinely evicted the untouched frame, not the one just re-accessed since the last sweep

items.item: This implementation's own CLOCK sweep bounds its search to twice the frame count before giving up, matching a real implementation's own need for a termination guarantee when every frame is pinned; this topic's own first claim already demonstrates that exact termination case.
